summary: In PIM-SM, routers keep mappings from multicast groups to a Rendezvous Point. This standards-track document updates how a router chooses among learned mappings, since the earlier algorithm didn't consider where each mapping came from. It makes the choice deterministic when several sources disagree.

eli5.summary: Many people may tell you who is in charge of a game, and their answers may differ. This gives routers a fair rule to pick one answer.

questions: how does pim choose a rendezvous point
subtitle: A fixed ten-step tie-breaking rule so every multicast router picks the same Rendezvous Point for a group.

tldr.problem: A PIM-SM router can learn several Group-to-RP mappings for the same multicast group from different sources, and the older selection algorithm ignores where a mapping came from and which PIM mode it is for. If routers pick different RPs, full multicast connectivity is not established.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a ten-step algorithm: embedded RP first, then longest prefix match, PIM mode (BIDIR over PIM-SM), origin (dynamic over static, BSR over Auto-RP), BSR priority, BSR hash, and finally the highest RP address as a tiebreaker.
tldr.outcome: Routers and management stations can now compute the same RP choice from the same set of mappings. The RFC updates RFC 4601 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6226 is a Proposed Standard from May 2011 that updates RFC 4601. It has not been obsoleted and no later RFC is listed as updating it.

sections.title: Why Routers Must Agree on the RP
sections.content:
In PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), each router keeps Group-to-RP mappings: a table that says which Rendezvous Point (RP) serves which multicast group address. Several mechanisms can create and distribute these mappings, so one router may learn more than one answer for the same group.

The RFC states that it is critical for every router to select the same RP for a given group address. Otherwise full multicast connectivity will not be established. This holds even with an Anycast RP: the address may map to different physical routers, but it is one logical RP address and must be consistent across the PIM domain. That is usually achieved by running the same selection algorithm in all routers of the domain.

The algorithm in RFC 4601 is not flexible enough for administrators to apply policies. The PIM-STD-MIB (RFC 5060) has a 'precedence' value, but because it is implementation-specific the MIB algorithm is not completely deterministic.
sections.eli5: Everyone playing a game must agree who the referee is. If two kids pick different referees, the game falls apart. This RFC makes sure everyone picks the same one.

sections.title: Terms and the Existing Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms. PIM Mode means either Sparse Mode or Bidirectional (BIDIR) Mode. Dynamic mappings are those learned by Bootstrap Router (BSR) or Auto-RP; mappings learned by Embedded-RP are called embedded mappings. A multicast domain is a network with a consistent set of mappings, and the edges between domains are multicast boundaries, usually enforced by filtering dynamic mapping messages or by configuring different static RP mappings.

The existing algorithm from Section 4.7.1 of RFC 4601 has two gaps. It treats all mappings equally regardless of origin, and it gives no way to prefer one PIM mode, so an entry learned for BIDIR is treated like one for PIM-SM.

The new algorithm is backward compatible and gives the same result only when mappings come from a single source. Its full benefits will not be realized until it is widely deployed.
sections.eli5: The old rule treated every answer as equally good, even when one came from a more trusted helper. The new rule notices who said it and what kind of game it is.

sections.title: Assumptions and Use Cases
sections.content:
The algorithm assumes this order of preference for how a mapping was learned, highest first: embedded mappings, dynamically learned mappings, static configuration, and any other method. Embedded mappings always win and cannot be overridden by static or dynamic mappings. A dynamic mapping overrides a static one with an overlapping range, though an operator can still override it by filtering or by configuring a longer static prefix. A mapping learned for BIDIR is preferred to one for PIM-SM, as stated in Section 3.3 of RFC 5059.

Three use cases motivate the work:

  • Default static mappings for the standard multicast range (224/4) combined with dynamically learned entries for specific applications, such as 239.100.0.0/16 for a corporate communications application.
  • Migrations after an acquisition or network redesign, where BSR and Auto-RP entries need deterministic handling to avoid interoperability surprises between vendors.
  • Management systems that run the algorithm on the mapping table fetched through MIB objects to find the RP a router will use for a group.
sections.eli5: Some helpers are trusted more than others, and a very specific note beats a general one. Grown-ups who run networks need a clear rule for this when they move from one setup to another.

sections.title: The Ten-Step Selection Algorithm
sections.content:
Section 6 narrows the candidate mappings step by step and stops as soon as one entry remains.

  1. If the group address contains an embedded RP, the RP address extracted from it is selected.
  2. If the group is in the Source Specific Multicast (SSM) range or configured for Dense Mode, no RP is selected and the algorithm ends.
  3. Keep only entries whose group prefix contains the group.
  4. If none remain, the mapping is undefined and the algorithm ends.
  5. Do a longest prefix match on the remaining entries.
  6. Prefer entries with PIM Mode BIDIR over PIM-SM.
  7. Prefer dynamically learned entries over static ones; between BSR and Auto-RP, prefer BSR.
  8. For BSR entries, compare the RP Priority from the Candidate-RP-Advertisement messages; the lowest value is the highest priority.
  9. For BSR entries in PIM-SM mode, use the hash function from Section 4.7.2 of RFC 4601; the highest hash value wins.
  10. As a final tiebreaker, select the RP with the numerically highest IP address.
sections.eli5: It is like a tournament with ten rounds. After each round, if only one contender is left, that one wins. If several tie, they play the next round, and the last round just picks the biggest number.

sections.title: Effect on MIB Objects
sections.content:
The PIM-STD-MIB (RFC 5060) summarizes mappings in the pimGroupMappingTable. The new algorithm does not use precedence, so the values of pimGroupMappingPrecedence and pimStaticRPPrecedence do not apply to it. They keep their meaning for legacy implementations, but are ignored on implementations that support the new algorithm.

An implementation can still be managed with the PIM-STD-MIB. Entries are created in pimGroupMappingTable for SSM and Dense Mode ranges, with pimGroupMappingRPAddressType set to unknown(0) and the PIM mode set to ssm(2) or dm(5). Entries already in the SSM Range table of the IP Multicast MIB (RFC 5132) are copied in with origin configSsm(3).
sections.eli5: The routers keep a notebook of who they think the leader is for each group. This part says how to write the notebook entries so that people checking it can follow the same rules.

sections.title: Operating Rules: Protocols, BIDIR and Filtering
sections.content:
Running several dynamic mapping mechanisms in one administrative domain is not usually necessary, and interoperation of BSR and Auto-RP is OPTIONAL. But if a router receives overlapping sets, this algorithm MUST be used on all routers in the domain. An implementation that supports only one mechanism MUST also use it; the RFC notes the algorithm was chosen so that existing standard implementations are already compliant.

For BIDIR-PIM (RFC 5015), the hash in BSR is ignored. The RFC RECOMMENDS that operators configure only one BIDIR RP for each RP Priority.

Implementations SHOULD support filtering of specific dynamic mechanisms for a valid group prefix range. For example, allowing the administratively scoped range 239/8 for Auto-RP while filtering the BSR advertisement for the same range, or filtering all mappings learned from BSR or Auto-RP.
sections.eli5: Pick one way of choosing leaders when you can. If two ways are used, everyone must follow the same rulebook, and borders can block messages they do not want.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Routers may select different mappings for the same group if the mappings they learned are not consistent. The RFC's example: if BSR is not enabled on one router, that router learns no BSR mappings and may choose a different RP, or none at all, for a group.

Such situations can be avoided if the mechanisms used to learn mappings are secure and consistent across the network. Secure transport of the mapping protocols can use IPsec authentication, as described in Section 6.3 of RFC 4601.
sections.eli5: If one router never hears one helper, it may pick a different leader. Keeping every helper's messages safe and the same for everybody prevents that.

viz.caption: THE TEN STEPS IN ORDER (RFC 6226 SECTION 6)

items.label: Embedded RP
items.desc: Use the RP address extracted from the group address.

items.label: SSM or Dense Mode
items.desc: No RP is selected; the algorithm ends.

items.label: Matching prefixes
items.desc: Keep entries whose prefix contains the group.

items.label: No entries
items.desc: The mapping is undefined; the algorithm ends.

items.label: Origin
items.desc: Dynamic over static; BSR over Auto-RP.

items.label: BSR RP Priority
items.desc: Lowest value is the highest priority.

items.label: Highest address
items.desc: Final tiebreaker: numerically greater IP address.
